title: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis

cards.explanation: Microbiome is used more broadly to include collective genes and activities.
cards.text: The organisms in a host-associated community are the {{c1::microbiota}}.
cards.question: The organisms in a host-associated community are the {{c1::microbiota}}.

cards.explanation: This is the distinction used in the lecture rather than treating both terms as exact synonyms.
cards.text: The microbiome includes microbial organisms plus their collective {{c1::genes and activities}}.
cards.question: The microbiome includes microbial organisms plus their collective {{c1::genes and activities}}.

cards.explanation: Local physical and chemical conditions influence which organisms persist.
cards.text: Different body sites support {{c1::distinct microbial communities}}.
cards.question: Different body sites support {{c1::distinct microbial communities}}.

cards.explanation: The source does not support the older universal claim of ten microbial cells per human cell.
cards.text: Human-associated microbial and human cell numbers are roughly of the {{c1::same order of magnitude}}.
cards.question: Human-associated microbial and human cell numbers are roughly of the {{c1::same order of magnitude}}.

cards.explanation: This is a distribution statement, not evidence that other sites are sterile.
cards.text: Most human-associated microbial biomass is found in the {{c1::colon}}.
cards.question: Most human-associated microbial biomass is found in the {{c1::colon}}.

cards.explanation: Traditional culture recovers only part of the community.
cards.text: Bacterial community profiling commonly uses the {{c1::16S rRNA gene}}.
cards.question: Bacterial community profiling commonly uses the {{c1::16S rRNA gene}}.

cards.explanation: This asks about genetic potential beyond identification by culture alone.
cards.text: Studying a community's collective genes and pathways uses {{c1::metagenomics}}.
cards.question: Studying a community's collective genes and pathways uses {{c1::metagenomics}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture marks the exact start of colonisation with a question mark; it should not be treated as proof of a healthy placental microbiome.
cards.text: Diet, antibiotics, environment and {{c1::age}} can change microbiome composition.
cards.question: Diet, antibiotics, environment and {{c1::age}} can change microbiome composition.

cards.explanation: This can provide usable metabolites from otherwise indigestible material.
cards.text: Gut microbes ferment dietary components that the host cannot fully {{c1::digest}}.
cards.question: Gut microbes ferment dietary components that the host cannot fully {{c1::digest}}.

cards.explanation: These metabolites can benefit the host rather than being merely waste products.
cards.text: Colonic fermentation produces {{c1::short-chain fatty acids}}.
cards.question: Colonic fermentation produces {{c1::short-chain fatty acids}}.

cards.explanation: Microbes and immune cells continually interact.
cards.text: Commensal microbes contribute to immune-system {{c1::development and regulation}}.
cards.question: Commensal microbes contribute to immune-system {{c1::development and regulation}}.

cards.explanation: Competition and inhibitory microbial products help maintain this protection.
cards.text: Protection against invading microbes by resident communities is {{c1::colonisation resistance}}.
cards.question: Protection against invading microbes by resident communities is {{c1::colonisation resistance}}.

cards.explanation: Loss of residents can open an ecological niche for opportunists.
cards.text: Resident microbes limit pathogen establishment by competing for nutrients and {{c1::attachment sites}}.
cards.question: Resident microbes limit pathogen establishment by competing for nutrients and {{c1::attachment sites}}.

cards.explanation: Competition is therefore not restricted to consumption of nutrients.
cards.text: Resident microbes may inhibit invaders by producing {{c1::antimicrobial compounds}}.
cards.question: Resident microbes may inhibit invaders by producing {{c1::antimicrobial compounds}}.

cards.explanation: Species and abundance vary across skin sites.
cards.text: Common skin-associated bacterial genera include Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium and {{c1::Cutibacterium}}.
cards.question: Common skin-associated bacterial genera include Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium and {{c1::Cutibacterium}}.

cards.explanation: Colonisation does not automatically equal active infection.
cards.text: A person may carry Staphylococcus aureus in the nose without {{c1::symptoms}}.
cards.question: A person may carry Staphylococcus aureus in the nose without {{c1::symptoms}}.

cards.explanation: The external auditory canal is a wax-rich microbial habitat.
cards.text: Disruption of external ear communities may contribute to {{c1::otitis externa}}.
cards.question: Disruption of external ear communities may contribute to {{c1::otitis externa}}.

cards.explanation: Low biomass does not mean that a sequencing signal automatically proves a stable resident community.
cards.text: Tear flow and antimicrobial compounds keep ocular microbial biomass relatively {{c1::low}}.
cards.question: Tear flow and antimicrobial compounds keep ocular microbial biomass relatively {{c1::low}}.

cards.explanation: Its organisation matters, rather than treating it as a random collection of free-floating cells.
cards.text: Dental plaque is a structured microbial {{c1::biofilm}}.
cards.question: Dental plaque is a structured microbial {{c1::biofilm}}.

cards.explanation: Microbial community disturbance can harm a normally colonised site.
cards.text: Oral dysbiosis contributes to caries and {{c1::periodontal disease}}.
cards.question: Oral dysbiosis contributes to caries and {{c1::periodontal disease}}.

cards.explanation: The rough tongue surface supports dense biofilms.
cards.text: Tongue-community disturbance may contribute to {{c1::halitosis}}.
cards.question: Tongue-community disturbance may contribute to {{c1::halitosis}}.

cards.explanation: The former blanket view of healthy lungs as sterile is oversimplified.
cards.text: Healthy lungs contain {{c1::low-biomass microbial communities}}.
cards.question: Healthy lungs contain {{c1::low-biomass microbial communities}}.

cards.explanation: Their detection must be interpreted in the context of biomass and sampling.
cards.text: Microorganisms reach the lungs by inhalation and {{c1::aspiration}}.
cards.question: Microorganisms reach the lungs by inhalation and {{c1::aspiration}}.

cards.explanation: There is biological variation between healthy individuals.
cards.text: Many healthy vaginal communities are dominated by {{c1::Lactobacillus}} species.
cards.question: Many healthy vaginal communities are dominated by {{c1::Lactobacillus}} species.

cards.explanation: The acidic environment contributes to resistance against some pathogens.
cards.text: Vaginal Lactobacillus helps maintain low pH by producing {{c1::lactic acid}}.
cards.question: Vaginal Lactobacillus helps maintain low pH by producing {{c1::lactic acid}}.

cards.explanation: Gut–brain signalling does not require microbes living in brain tissue.
cards.text: A stable resident microbiome has not been established in the healthy {{c1::brain}}.
cards.question: A stable resident microbiome has not been established in the healthy {{c1::brain}}.

cards.explanation: Odour can reflect microbial activity rather than sweat alone.
cards.text: Many axillary body odours result from bacterial metabolism of {{c1::sweat-derived compounds}}.
cards.question: Many axillary body odours result from bacterial metabolism of {{c1::sweat-derived compounds}}.

cards.explanation: Nail crevices can carry both transient and resident organisms.
cards.text: Handwashing should include the {{c1::fingernails}} because microbes can become trapped beneath them.
cards.question: Handwashing should include the {{c1::fingernails}} because microbes can become trapped beneath them.

cards.explanation: Footwear and moisture alter the local environment.
cards.text: The fungal group linked to toenail disease in the lecture is {{c1::dermatophytes}}.
cards.question: The fungal group linked to toenail disease in the lecture is {{c1::dermatophytes}}.

cards.explanation: This is a fungal genus, illustrating that the microbiota is not exclusively bacterial.
cards.text: The lecture includes Malassezia among {{c1::hair/scalp-associated}} microbes.
cards.question: The lecture includes Malassezia among {{c1::hair/scalp-associated}} microbes.

cards.explanation: Helicobacter pylori can persist in some individuals despite this barrier.
cards.text: The stomach's {{c1::acidity}} limits its microbial biomass.
cards.question: The stomach's {{c1::acidity}} limits its microbial biomass.

cards.explanation: Different intestinal regions are distinct ecological niches.
cards.text: Rapid transit, bile salts and digestive enzymes help keep small-intestinal density lower than the {{c1::colon}}.
cards.question: Rapid transit, bile salts and digestive enzymes help keep small-intestinal density lower than the {{c1::colon}}.

cards.explanation: Local oxygen availability helps explain community composition.
cards.text: The oxygen-poor colon favours {{c1::anaerobic bacteria}}.
cards.question: The oxygen-poor colon favours {{c1::anaerobic bacteria}}.

cards.explanation: The historic assumption that every healthy urinary site is sterile is too broad.
cards.text: Healthy bladders can harbour microbial {{c1::communities}}.
cards.question: Healthy bladders can harbour microbial {{c1::communities}}.

cards.explanation: The source notes DNA and viable organisms in urine; sampling, symptoms and clinical context matter.
cards.text: Finding microbial DNA does not by itself establish {{c1::infection}}.
cards.question: Finding microbial DNA does not by itself establish {{c1::infection}}.

cards.explanation: Detection during infection does not establish a normal resident community.
cards.text: No reliable resident microbiome has been demonstrated in healthy {{c1::kidneys}}.
cards.question: No reliable resident microbiome has been demonstrated in healthy {{c1::kidneys}}.

cards.explanation: This gut–liver interaction does not establish a healthy resident liver microbiome.
cards.text: Gut microbial products can reach the liver through the {{c1::circulation}}.
cards.question: Gut microbial products can reach the liver through the {{c1::circulation}}.

cards.explanation: A low-biomass signal needs careful controls; microbes in blood can indicate infection.
cards.text: Claims of a normal blood microbiome are confounded by sampling {{c1::contamination}}.
cards.question: Claims of a normal blood microbiome are confounded by sampling {{c1::contamination}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture supports no established normal resident placental microbiome in healthy pregnancies.
cards.text: Many reported placental microbiome signals were attributed to {{c1::contamination}}.
cards.question: Many reported placental microbiome signals were attributed to {{c1::contamination}}.

cards.explanation: This can include loss of beneficial organisms and overgrowth of others.
cards.text: Disruption of a usual microbial community is called {{c1::dysbiosis}}.
cards.question: Disruption of a usual microbial community is called {{c1::dysbiosis}}.

cards.explanation: An opportunist can exploit the resulting ecological space.
cards.text: Broad-spectrum antibiotics can weaken colonisation resistance by reducing community {{c1::diversity}}.
cards.question: Broad-spectrum antibiotics can weaken colonisation resistance by reducing community {{c1::diversity}}.

cards.explanation: Barrier disruption, site change or overgrowth can allow a resident organism to cause disease.
cards.text: Infection arising from an organism already carried by the host is {{c1::endogenous infection}}.
cards.question: Infection arising from an organism already carried by the host is {{c1::endogenous infection}}.

cards.explanation: Disease may change the microbiome, or both may share another cause.
cards.text: An association between dysbiosis and disease does not prove {{c1::causation}}.
cards.question: An association between dysbiosis and disease does not prove {{c1::causation}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture highlights recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection as an important application.
cards.text: FMT transfers donor {{c1::stool microbiota}} to a recipient.
cards.question: FMT transfers donor {{c1::stool microbiota}} to a recipient.

cards.explanation: This supports the importance of restoring community structure; FMT requires clinical screening and supervision.
cards.text: The recurrent infection highlighted as responsive to FMT is {{c1::Clostridioides difficile infection}}.
cards.question: The recurrent infection highlighted as responsive to FMT is {{c1::Clostridioides difficile infection}}.

cards.explanation: They differ from substrates supplied to support resident microbial growth.
cards.text: Probiotics aim to introduce beneficial {{c1::microorganisms}}.
cards.question: Probiotics aim to introduce beneficial {{c1::microorganisms}}.

cards.explanation: They are not themselves the live organisms supplied by probiotics.
cards.text: Prebiotics supply substrates that selectively support microbial {{c1::growth}}.
cards.question: Prebiotics supply substrates that selectively support microbial {{c1::growth}}.

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 1
slides.text:
LS5008/30 – The Human Microbiome
Dr Lewis C. E. MasonBSc (Hons), MSc, PhD, AFHEA, MRSB

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 2
slides.text:
Learning objectives
Recall the different sites of the human bodywhere microbes are found, and examplesof microbes at each

Explain how endogenous infection may occur

Critically evaluate the advantages anddisadvantages of microbial presence

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 3
slides.text: Starter activity – Guess Who?

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 4
slides.text:
What is the microbiome?
Distinction between microbiota (the organisms) and microbiome(+ their collective genes and activities)

Different body sites harbour distinct microbial communities 

Most microorganisms associated with humans are harmless or even beneficial

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 5
slides.text:
How many are we carrying?
The human body contains approximately as many microbial cells as human cells
Most microbial biomass is located within the large intestine (colon)

The collective genetic content of themicrobiome greatly exceeds that of the human genome

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 6
slides.text:
How is the microbiome researched?
Traditional culture techniquesrecover only a subset of microbialdiversity

16S rRNA gene sequencing permitsbacterial community profiling
Metagenomics allows identification ofgenes and metabolic pathways

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 7
slides.text:
Establishment of the Microbiome
Colonisation begins at birth(?) and changes rapidly during infancy

Diet, environment, antibiotics, and age influence microbial composition

Adult microbiomes are relatively stable but still remain dynamic

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 8
slides.text:
The gastrointestinal tract
The GI tract contains the largest microbialpopulation in the body

Dominant bacterial phyla include Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes

Gut microorganisms contribute tonutrient metabolism

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 9
slides.text:
Functions of the gut microbiome
Fermentation of otherwise indigestible dietary components

Production of vitamins and short-chain fatty acids

Contribution to immune system development and regulation

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 10
slides.text:
Colonisation resistance
Resident microbiota compete withpathogens for nutrients and attachment sites

Production of antimicrobial compounds can inhibit invading microbes

A healthy microbiome reduces susceptibility to infection

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 11
slides.text:
The Skin Microbiome
Different skin sites supportdistinct microbial communities

Common genera include:Staphylococcus, Cutibacterium,Corynebacterium

Skin-associated microbes contributeto barrier defence

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 12
slides.text:
The Nose Microbiome
The nasal cavity serves as an important reservoir for respiratory microorganisms

Common inhabitants include Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium, and Moraxella spp.

Some individuals are persistent carriers of Staphylococcus aureus without signs of disease

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 13
slides.text:
The Ear Microbiome
The external auditory canal supportsmicrobial communities adapted to a wax-rich environment

Common residents include Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium, and Cutibacterium species

Disruption of the normal ear microbiota may contribute to otitis externa

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 14
slides.text:
The Eye Microbiome
The ocular surface carries fewmicroorganisms due to tear flow andantimicrobial compounds

Common genera include Staphylococcus,Corynebacterium, and Cutibacterium

Resident microorganisms contribute to ocular homeostasis and pathogen exclusion

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 15
slides.text:
The Oral Microbiome
The mouth contains highlydiverse microbial biofilms

Dental plaque represents a structured microbial community
Dysbiosis contributes to dentalcaries and periodontal disease

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 16
slides.text:
The Tongue Microbiome
The tongue provides a rough surfacethat supports dense, highly structured biofilms 

Common genera include Streptococcus, Veillonella, Actinomyces, Neisseria,and Prevotella spp.

Dysbiosis may contribute to halitosis (bad breath)

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 17
slides.text:
The Lung Microbiome
The lungs were once thought to be sterile, but healthy lungs contain low-biomass microbial communities

Microorganisms reach the lungs through inhalation and aspiration

Changes in the lung microbiome are associated with asthma, COPD, and cystic fibrosis

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 18
slides.text:
The Vaginal Microbiome
Many healthy communitiesare dominated by Lactobacillusspp.

Lactic acid production contributesto the low pH environment

Changes in microbiome canpredispose to disease

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 19
slides.text:
The Brain Microbiome(?)
The healthy brain is generally considered a sterile site

No stable resident brain microbiome has been demonstrated in healthy individuals
The gut microbiome may influence brain function via the gut-brain axis

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 20
slides.text:
The Armpit Microbiome
The axilla is rich in sweat glands and supports dense microbial populations
Dominant genera often include Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus

Many body odours are produced by bacterial metabolism of sweat-derived compounds

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 21
slides.text:
The Umbilical Microbiome
The umbilicus provides a warm, sheltered environment that supportsdiverse microbial communities
Hundreds of bacterial species have been identified from human navels
The composition of the umbilical microbiome varies substantially betweenindviduals

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 22
slides.text:
The Fingernail Microbiome
Fingernails provide crevices that can trap microorganisms from the environment

Both transient and resident microorganisms may be present beneath the nails 

Effective handwashing should include scrubbing the fingernails

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 23
slides.text:
The Toenail Microbiome
Toenails support bacterial and fungal populations influenced by footwear and moisture

Dermatophyte fungi may colonise toenails and contribute to disease

The toenail microbiome differs substantially from that found on nearby skin sites

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 24
slides.text:
The Hair Microbiome
Hair shafts and hair follicles supportdistinct microbial communities

Common residents include Cutibacterium, Staphylococcus, and Malassezia spp.

Follicular microorganisms can influence scalp health and inflammatory conditions

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 25
slides.text:
The Stomach Microbiome
The stomach contains relatively low microbial biomass due to its highly acidic environment (pH 1-3)

Despite this, diverse microorganisms can be detected, including Helicobacter pylori in some individuals

Gastric acidity acts as a barrier preventing many microorganisms

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 26
slides.text:
The Small Intestine Microbiome
Microbial density is lower than in the colon because of the rapid transit, bile salts, and digestive enzymes 

Common inhabitants include Streptococcus, Lactobacillus, and Enterococcus species

Small intestinal microorganisms contribute to nutrient metabolism and immune function

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 27
slides.text:
The Colon Microbiome
The colon contains the highest microbial density in the human body 

Anaerobic bacteria dominate due to the oxygen-poor environment

Colonic microorganisms ferment dietary fibre to produce short-chain fatty acids that benefit the host

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 28
slides.text:
The Bladder Microbiome
The bladder was historically considered sterile, but we now know it harbours microbial communities in many individuals

Common genera include Lactobacillus, Gardnerella, Streptococcus, Corynebacterium

Alterations in the bladder biome may influence susceptibility to UTIs

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 29
slides.text:
The Urinary Microbiome (Urine)
Urine was traditionally regarded as sterile in healthy individuals

Modern sequencing techniques have detected microbial DNA and viable organisms in many urine samples

The composition of urinary microbial communities varies between individuals and may influence urinary health

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 30
slides.text:
The Kidney Microbiome(?)
Healthy kidneys are generally considered to be sterile organs 

No resident kidney microbiome has been reliably demonstrated 

Microorganisms may be detected during UTIs or systemic bloodstream infections

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 31
slides.text:
The Liver Microbiome(?)
The liver is generally considered a sterile organ under healthy conditions. Microbial products from the gut reach the liver via circulation. Interactions between the gut microbiome and liver contribute to the gut-liver axis

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 32
slides.text:
The Blood Microbiome(?)
Healthy blood has traditionally been considered sterile

Claims of a “blood microbiome” remain hotly controversial and are complicated by issues of contamination during sampling 

Detection of microbes in the blood is usually interpreted as evidence of infection

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 33
slides.text:
The Placental Microbiome(?)
Earlier studies suggested that the placenta might contain a unique microbiome 

Subsequent studies indicated many findings were likely due to contamination

Current evidence generally supports the placenta being sterile in healthy pregnancies

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 34
slides.text:
Microbiome and the Immune System
Continuous interactions occurbetween microbes and immune cells

Commensal microorganisms promote immune maturation

Dysregulated interactions can contribute to inflammation

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 35
slides.text:
What is Dysbiosis?
Dysbiosis refers to disruption of the ‘normal’ microbial community
Loss of beneficial organismsmay allow pathogen overgrowth
Dysbiosis is associated with many diseases

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 36
slides.text:
Antibiotics and the Microbiome
Broad-spectrum antibiotics cansubstantially alter microbialcommunities

Reduction in diversity may increasesusceptibility to opportunistic pathogens

Recovery of the microbiome can take months

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 37
slides.text:
Microbiome and InfectiousDisease
Disruption of normal microbiotacan increase infection risk

Some pathogens exploit ecologicalniches created by dysbiosis

The microbiome can influence pathogen colonisation success

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 38
slides.text:
Links Between the Microbiomeand Chronic Disease
Associations have been reportedwith obesity, inflammatory bowel disease, and diabetes

Altered microbial metabolites may influence host physiology

Association does not necessarily imply causation… reverse causality?

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 39
slides.text:
Faecal MicrobiotaTransplantation (FMT)
This is the transfer of stool from ‘healthy’ donors to recipients

It is highly effective for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection

Demonstrates the importance of microbial community structure

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 40
slides.text:
Can we manipulate themicrobiome?
Probiotics aim to introduce beneficialmicroorganisms

Prebiotics provide substrates that selectively support microbial growth

Dietary interventions may altermicrobiome composition

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 41
slides.text:
Future directions in Microbiome Research
Personalised medicine based onmicrobiome profiling?

Development of targeted microbiome therapeutics?

Better understanding of host-microbeinteractions (the gut-brain axis)?

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 42
slides.text:
Plenary activity
Imagine that you are designing aprobiotic product…

What factors do you need to considerin its development?

slides.topic: The Human Microbiome — Communities, Protection & Dysbiosis — source 43
slides.text:
Summary
Humans are ecosystems containingdiverse microbial communities

Microbiota contribute to nutrition, immunity,and pathogen resistance

Alteration of microbial communities can influencehealth and disease
